title: Preity Zinta Just Got Permission to Take Google and Meta to Court Over AI Deepfakes. The Dimpled Smile Is Done Being Polite.
excerpt: The Bombay High Court has cleared Bollywood's eternal sweetheart to sue the tech giants over deepfake videos, doctored images and AI chatbots built from her face. She's the latest star to fight back — and the suit could reshape who owns a celebrity's likeness in India.
body:
For thirty years, **Preity Zinta** has been Bollywood's most disarming presence — the dimpled, jet-fuelled energy of *Dil Se*, *Kal Ho Naa Ho* and *Veer-Zaara*, the woman who could make a single grin carry an entire frame. This week she walked into the Bombay High Court wearing a very different expression, and the tech world should be paying attention.

On Tuesday, June 16, Justice **Abhay Ahuja** granted Zinta permission to file a substantive civil suit against **Google LLC**, **Meta Platforms** and a string of other websites and platforms over what she alleges is a flood of AI-generated deepfake content built from her likeness — fake videos, manipulated images, memes, and even AI chatbot "personas" impersonating her. The case is formally titled *Preity Zinta v. Google LLC & Ors*, and the order, reported first by Bar and Bench, lets her case proceed on the original side of the High Court.

The legal mechanics are drier than the headline, but they matter. Zinta's counsel, advocate **Rohan Kadam** (briefed by B Munim & Co), sought leave under Clause XII of the Letters Patent — a procedural step required when part of the cause of action arises outside the court's territorial jurisdiction. Because the offending content lives on servers and platforms scattered worldwide, Zinta had to convince the judge that her goodwill, reputation and persona are "situate" in Mumbai, where she lives and works. Justice Ahuja agreed, accepting that her reputation is anchored in the city even if the deepfakes are global.

> "She contends the content amounts to a breach of her personality rights, infringement of copyright, and a violation of her moral rights under the Copyright Act."

What she's actually claiming is sweeping. The suit alleges breach of her **personality rights**, infringement of copyright, erosion of "immense goodwill and reputation," and a violation of her moral rights under Section 62 of the Copyright Act, 1957. In plain terms: she is arguing that her face, her voice and her digital self belong to her, and that no one — not a meme account, not a chatbot, not a platform that hosts them — gets to monetise or distort them without consent.

Zinta is not fighting this battle alone, and that's what makes it consequential. Over the past two years, the Bombay High Court has become the unlikely epicentre of India's personality-rights reckoning, granting relief to a roll call of stars: **Akshay Kumar**, **Shilpa Shetty**, **Kartik Aaryan**, **Shatrughan Sinha** and **Suniel Shetty** — the last of whom went to court after a deepfake image surfaced pairing him with his infant granddaughter. Down south, **Naga Chaitanya** has pursued a parallel case. A pattern is hardening into precedent, and Indian courts are increasingly willing to treat a celebrity's likeness as property worth protecting.

For the diaspora, this is more than gossip-page fodder. NRIs are among the heaviest consumers — and unwitting sharers — of exactly the kind of AI-manipulated content these suits target; the doctored clip forwarded on a family WhatsApp group in Houston or Hounslow is the everyday face of this problem. And the defendants are American giants. A ruling that pins liability on Google or Meta for content generated and circulated on their platforms would ripple far beyond Bollywood, touching the same debates over AI, consent and likeness now raging in Hollywood and Silicon Valley.

Zinta, for her part, has always been the rare Bollywood star who reinvented herself off-screen — co-owner of the IPL's Punjab Kings, a businesswoman, a mother of twins who relocated her life to Los Angeles years ago. She knows the American tech ecosystem intimately, which may be precisely why she's unafraid to take its biggest names to court. The substantive suit — seeking an injunction and other reliefs — will now proceed independently before the High Court.

The dimpled smile built a career on warmth. But this fight is about something colder and more modern: in an age when anyone's face can be conjured, distorted and sold by a machine, who actually owns it? Zinta has decided the answer is her — and she's got a courtroom ready to hear it.
